> The primary goal of Experiment 1 is to replicate the associational blocking
effect observed by @beesley2011 in a large-scale online sample, to ensure the
effect is replicable in our research setting before trying to extend the
original findings.

::: {.callout-tip title="Goals"}
In this report, the aims are to:

1. **inform expectations** about the true effect size, from the literature and
   from the feasibility study,
2. **conduct a formal power analysis** of the original index (BI~2~) to estimate
   a sufficient sample size, and evaluate the power of the alternative index
   (BI~3~) at that sample size,
3. **set the rules** for declaring (non-)replication and for the
   group-sequential top-up of the sample if needed.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="90% confidence intervals"}
Because the replication study `fba-allergy-online-02` aims to detect blocking
in a design for which there is a strong theoretical justification for expecting
its direction *a priori*, the study pre-registers and employs a one-sided *t*-test
with the alternative hypothesis of the effect being greater than zero.
Consequently, all effect size estimates presented in this notebook are
accompanied by their **90% confidence intervals** (CIs), not 95% CIs, as the
former align better with the one-sided test.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="R code: Set-up"}
```{r}
#| label: replication-pwr-envir
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(tidyverse)
  library(gt)
  library(pwrss)
})

# Search files in relation to the project repository directory, so that the
# code remains renderable no matter where it is called from
REPO <- rprojroot::find_root(rprojroot::has_file("CATLAS.Rproj"))

# Formatting helpers shared by all manuscripts
source(file.path(REPO, "common", "R", "utils-print.R"))

# Tables and helpers of this notebook
source(file.path(REPO, "manuscripts", "forward-blocking-attention-01", "R", "03-replication-power.R"))

# Because the replication aims to detect an effect in the predicted direction
# at the 5% level of significance, alpha for CIs is set at 0.10, i.e., 90% CIs,
# which align with this aim better than the typical 95% CIs.
alpha_ci <- .10
```
:::

# Effect size of blocking

## Prior literature

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="R code: Literature-based effect size estimates"}
```{r}
#| label: replication-pwr-literature
# Reported tests of blocking in experiments similar to the one being replicated,
# one row per experiment. The F-test of Le Pelley et al. (2007) has one
# numerator degree of freedom, i.e., it is equivalent to a squared paired t-test
literature <- tibble::tribble(
  ~study,            ~index, ~test, ~statistic, ~n,
  "beesley2011",     "BI2",  "t",   2.74,       26L,
  "lepelley2007",    "BI1",  "F",   7.00,       8L,
  "griffiths2009e1", "BI1",  "t",   2.07,       32L,
  "griffiths2009e3", "BI3",  "t",   5.03,       40L
)

# Cohen's d_z with its CI, and the two-sided p-value of each reported test
lit <-
  literature |>
  standardise_reported_tests(level = 1 - alpha_ci) |>
  split(~ study)

# Raw effect magnitude of Beesley and Le Pelley (2011), with the standard
# deviation implied by their test
x_bar <- 2.03
s <- x_bar * sqrt(lit$beesley2011$n) / lit$beesley2011$t
se <- s / sqrt(lit$beesley2011$n)
ci_low <- x_bar - stats::qt(alpha_ci / 2, lit$beesley2011$df, lower.tail = FALSE) * se
ci_upp <- x_bar + stats::qt(alpha_ci / 2, lit$beesley2011$df, lower.tail = FALSE) * se
```
:::

### @beesley2011

@beesley2011 employed the 2AFC *negation test* [@don2018] to measure blocking
and reported mean blocking index[^1] $\mathbb{E}(BI_2) = +2.03$ across their
sample of *N* = 26 participants. After conducting a one-sample two-sided
*t*-test against the null hypothesis $\mathbb{E}(BI_2) = 0$, they concluded that
the observed difference is significantly different from zero, *t*(25) = 2.74,
*p* = .011.

[^1]: See the [Dependent Variables](01-estimands-estimates.qmd) notebook for
definition of BI~2~ and other blocking indices used to estimate the effect of
blocking in contingency learning experimental paradigms.

Although the authors do not directly provide estimates of effect variance and
its standardised size, these metrics can be deduced from the information about
the raw effect magnitude and *t*-test results.

Firstly, the effect's standard deviation can be calculated from the test
statistic, raw effect magnitude, and sample size:

$$t = \frac{\bar{X}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt{N}}$$
$$2.74 = \frac{2.03-0}{s/\sqrt{26}}$$
$$s = \frac{2.03\sqrt{26}}{2.74} \approx 3.78$$

Secondly, the standardised effect size, Cohen's *d*~z~ (the mean divided by the
standard deviation), follows as:

$$d_z = \frac{\bar{X}}{s} = \frac{t}{\sqrt{N}} = \frac{2.74}{\sqrt{26}} \approx 0.54$$

Together, these result in:

- Raw effect magnitude:
  $\bar{X} = `r x_bar` \ `r print_ci(ci_low, ci_upp)`$
- Standardised effect size:
  $d_z = `r print_d(lit$beesley2011$d)` \ `r print_ci(lit$beesley2011$d_low, lit$beesley2011$d_high)`$

### Other studies

To further evaluate the most likely values of the true effect size, one might
look at experiments similar to the one aimed to be replicated. Papers most
similar in their experimental design to @beesley2011 are @lepelley2007 and
@griffiths2009. The former introduced the three-stage design in its current form
to address potential competing explanations such as memory interference, while
the latter extended the design to evaluate to what degree the blocking
effect depends on the presence of the original blocking stimulus in Stage 3
learning.

#### @lepelley2007

@lepelley2007 measured blocking using a BI~1~ type of blocking index, with the
exception that instead of evaluating predictive value of each cue separately,
cue compounds including either two blocked or two control cues associated with
the same outcome were used. In a total of `r lit$lepelley2007$n` participants,
they observed a statistically significant blocking effect,
*F*(1, `r lit$lepelley2007$df`) = `r lit$lepelley2007$statistic`,
*p* `r print_p(lit$lepelley2007$p)`, translating to
$d_z = `r print_d(lit$lepelley2007$d)` \ `r print_ci(lit$lepelley2007$d_low, lit$lepelley2007$d_high)`$.

#### @griffiths2009

@griffiths2009 measured blocking of the same structure, i.e., comparing blocked
cues with novel control cues after Stage 3 learning, in their Experiments 1 and
3.[^2]

[^2]: Their Experiment 2, although using 2AFC *negation test* with a BI~3~-like
measure of blocking, omits the critical blocked cue vs. novel control cue
comparisons.

In Experiment 1, the effect was measured using BI~1~. Based on data from
`r lit$griffiths2009e1$n` participants, @griffiths2009 observed a statistically
significant blocking effect,
*t*(`r lit$griffiths2009e1$df`) = `r lit$griffiths2009e1$statistic`,
*p* `r print_p(lit$griffiths2009e1$p)`, translating to
$d_z = `r print_d(lit$griffiths2009e1$d)` \ `r print_ci(lit$griffiths2009e1$d_low, lit$griffiths2009e1$d_high)`$.

Most relevantly, Experiment 3 of @griffiths2009 estimates blocking using a 2AFC
*negation test* procedure similar to that used by @beesley2011, employing an
estimate similar to BI~3~ based on two test blocks per participant. Based on
data from `r lit$griffiths2009e3$n` participants, @griffiths2009 observed a
statistically significant blocking effect,
*t*(`r lit$griffiths2009e3$df`) = `r lit$griffiths2009e3$statistic`,
*p* `r print_p(lit$griffiths2009e3$p)`, translating to
$d_z = `r print_d(lit$griffiths2009e3$d)` \ `r print_ci(lit$griffiths2009e3$d_low, lit$griffiths2009e3$d_high)`$.

### Summary

The effect sizes observed in experiments similar to @beesley2011 vary widely.
Two of them come with large uncertainty [@lepelley2007] or a relatively small
effect whose 90% CI sits near zero [@griffiths2009, Exp. 1]. Admittedly,
both used BI~1~ as their measure of blocking, which may be less sensitive to
blocking than BI~2~ or BI~3~. Experiment 3 of @griffiths2009 used a BI~3~-like
index and yielded a relatively large effect, larger than the one observed by
@beesley2011.

| Study | Measure | *d*~z~ [90% CI] |
|:------|:-----|:--------------------|
| ***@beesley2011*** | ***BI~2~*** | ***`r print_d(lit$beesley2011$d)` `r print_ci(lit$beesley2011$d_low, lit$beesley2011$d_high)`*** |
| @lepelley2007 | BI~1~ | `r print_d(lit$lepelley2007$d)` `r print_ci(lit$lepelley2007$d_low, lit$lepelley2007$d_high)` |
| @griffiths2009, Exp. 1 | BI~1~ | `r print_d(lit$griffiths2009e1$d)` `r print_ci(lit$griffiths2009e1$d_low, lit$griffiths2009e1$d_high)` |
| @griffiths2009, Exp. 3 | BI~3~ | `r print_d(lit$griffiths2009e3$d)` `r print_ci(lit$griffiths2009e3$d_low, lit$griffiths2009e3$d_high)` |

## Feasibility study

The second type of evidence considered here for setting a realistic value of the
true effect size for the prospective power analysis comes from the feasibility
study `fba-allergy-online-01`. During it, I ran the three-stage design of
@beesley2011 using the modified allergist task online. Its results are reported
in full in the [Feasibility Study](02-feasibility-study.qmd) notebook. The
analysis was conducted on three analysis data sets with increasingly tighter
exclusion criteria:

1. the **Full sample** excluded only participants without sufficient
   experimental data,
2. the **Learned set** additionally excluded participants failing the learning
   check, and
3. the **Naive set** also excluded participants claiming to know the
   experiment.

For reasons explained below, the Learned and Naive sets swap their roles for the
replication study.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="R code: Feasibility estimates"}
```{r}
#| label: replication-pwr-feasibility
# Pilot estimates and attrition funnel, saved by `02-feasibility-study.qmd`
estimates <- read_output("02-feasibility-estimates.rds", REPO)
funnel <- read_output("02-feasibility-funnel.rds", REPO)

# The original index (BI2 on test block 1) and the alternative index (BI3 over
# all test blocks) in each of the three analysis sets, tested one-sided with
# two-sided 90% CIs
sets <- c(
  full    = "1 \u00b7 Full sample",
  learned = "2 \u00b7 Learned",
  naive   = "3 \u00b7 Naive"
)
stopifnot(
  setequal(as.character(estimates$set), sets),
  nrow(estimates) == 6L,
  all(estimates$alternative == "greater"),
  isTRUE(all.equal(unique(estimates$perc), 1 - alpha_ci))
)

d_bi2 <- purrr::map_dbl(sets, \(s) {
  pick_estimate(estimates, s, "bi_confidence")
})

d_bi3 <- purrr::map_dbl(sets, \(s) {
  pick_estimate(estimates, s, "bi_choice")
})

n_sets <- purrr::map_dbl(sets, \(s) {
  pick_estimate(estimates, s, "bi_confidence", "n")
})

# Every interval must cover no blocking and the effect size of Beesley and
# Le Pelley (2011), as the text says
stopifnot(
  all(estimates$d_low < 0),
  all(estimates$d_high > lit$beesley2011$d)
)

# Point estimates of BI3 as range for text
bi3_range <- print_range(c(d_bi3[["learned"]], d_bi3[["full"]]))

# Prepare estimates for a table
prep_estimates <- prepare_pilot_estimates(estimates)
```
:::

::: {.callout-important title="The Learned and the Naive set swap roles"}
| Set | Exclusions | Feasibility | Replication |
|:--|:----|:--|:--|
| 1 · Full sample | structural only | sensitivity | sensitivity |
| 2 · Learned | structural, learning check | **primary** | sensitivity |
| 3 · Naive | structural, learning check, prior knowledge | sensitivity | **primary** |

The table shows each analysis set used in the feasibility study and planned to
be used in the replication study, together with their role in each analysis. The
Naive set leaves out participants who report prior knowledge of similar
experiments, and may thus answer according to what they expect the study to show
rather than according to what they learned. In the feasibility study, the
primary analysis set kept these participants
(*n* = `r n_sets[["learned"]] - n_sets[["naive"]]`).

In `fba-allergy-online-02`, the debriefing question becomes a two-parter (asking
about prior experiments of the same kind, and critically adding a question about
knowing or guessing what the study tested) and the Naive set becomes the primary
analysis set.
:::

### Effect size estimates

In the Full sample and the Learned set, BI~2~ on the first test block yielded
*d*~z~ of `r print_d(d_bi2[["full"]])` and `r print_d(d_bi2[["learned"]])`,
respectively, and BI~3~ over all test blocks `r print_d(d_bi3[["full"]])`
and `r print_d(d_bi3[["learned"]])`. In the naive set, both effect sizes were cut
to about half or less (`r print_d(d_bi2[["naive"]])` for BI~2~,
`r print_d(d_bi3[["naive"]])` for BI~3~). None of the one-sided tests rejected
the null hypothesis of no blocking, and every 90% CI includes both zero and
the original study's estimate *d*~z~ &approx; `r print_d(lit$beesley2011$d)` (see the
table below).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-replication-pwr-feasibility
#| tbl-cap: "Effect size estimates of the feasibility study (`fba-allergy-online-01`) per analysis set."
tbl_pilot_estimates(prep_estimates, 1 - alpha_ci)
```

### Retention

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="R code: Retention"}
```{r}
#| label: replication-pwr-retention
retention <- summarise_retention(funnel, "Total")

# The three steps that removed participants in the pilot
stopifnot(identical(
  retention$step,
  c("Incomplete run", "Insufficient learning", "Prior knowledge")
))
yield <- stats::setNames(
  retention$yield,
  retention$step
)

n_records <- funnel$Total[1L]
n_learned <- funnel$Total[nrow(funnel) - 1L]
n_naive <- funnel$Total[nrow(funnel)]
n_records_labels <- funnel$LABELS[1L]
n_naive_labels <- funnel$LABELS[nrow(funnel)]

# Retention if no run were incomplete
yield_complete <- prod(yield[c("Insufficient learning", "Prior knowledge")])

# Prepare funnel data for table
prep_funnel <- prepare_retention(funnel)
```
:::

Of the `r print_num_word(n_records, TRUE)` JATOS records of the feasibility
study, `r print_num_word(n_learned, TRUE)`
(`r round(100 * n_learned / n_records)`%)
reached the Learned set, and `r print_num_word(n_naive)`
(`r round(100 * n_naive / n_records)`%)
reached the Naive set (see the table below).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-replication-pwr-retention
#| tbl-cap: "Participant retention through the exclusion steps of the feasibility study, over all recruitment channels and in the LABELS channel specifically."
tbl_retention(prep_funnel)
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Assumed retention for the `fba-allergy-online-02` study"}
Following the retention rates observed in the feasibility study, I assume
50% retention for `fba-allergy-online-02`, i.e., that half of the participants
who start the experiment will be included in the Naive set, the primary analysis
set of the study. The assumption stems from three observations:

- **Incomplete runs**, because of which
  `r print_n_pct(retention$before[1L] - retention$after[1L], n_records)`
  records were excluded, should become rarer. Both incomplete runs of the LABELS
  channel were lost due to unstable internet connections, which is an issue that
  will be solved in the new experimental code (`catlaslab` issue #9).
- **Without incomplete runs**, the yields of the learning check
  (`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * yield[["Insufficient learning"]])`) and of the
  prior-knowledge exclusion
  (`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * yield[["Prior knowledge"]])`) multiply to
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * yield_complete)`.
- **In the LABELS channel**, from which `fba-allergy-online-02` recruits,
  `r print_n_pct(n_naive_labels, n_records_labels)` records reached the Naive
  set.
:::

## Assumed true effect size

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="R code: Effect size scenarios"}
```{r}
#| label: replication-pwr-scenarios
# The three scenarios, rounded to two decimals as in the text: the original
# study, the lower of the two main estimates of the feasibility study (the Full
# sample), and its Naive set
d_best <- round(lit$beesley2011$d, 2)
d_real <- round(d_bi2[["full"]], 2)
d_worst <- round(d_bi2[["naive"]], 2)

stopifnot(d_bi2[["full"]] <= d_bi2[["learned"]])

# Schäfer & Schwarz (2019) correlation estimates converted to d
r_schafer <- c(0.16, 0.36)
d_schafer <- 2 * r_schafer / sqrt(1 - r_schafer^2)
```
:::

The prospective power analysis below combines the estimate of @beesley2011
with those of the feasibility study into three scenarios:

| Scenario | *d*~z~ | Reason |
|:--|:-:|:---------|
| *Worst* | `r d_worst` | Feasibility study's Naive set estimate, an effect size considered to be small [cf. @lovakov2021] |
| *Realistic* | `r d_real` | The lower of the feasibility study's Full sample and Learned set estimates, an effect size considered to be medium [cf. @lovakov2021] |
| *Best* | `r d_best` | The point estimate of the original study [@beesley2011], an effect size between medium and large [cf. @lovakov2021] |

::: {.callout-important title="Effect size magnitude interpretation"}
The size labels used in this notebook follow the empirically derived benchmarks
of @lovakov2021, who set small, medium and large effects at *d* = 0.15, 0.36 and
0.65, respectively. These serve only as a rough guide here, because of the exact
field they were derived from (social psychology, not learning, experimental or
cognitive psychology), and the fact they describe standardised differences
between groups or conditions, whose scale differs from that of *d*~z~, which is
the mean of a within-participant index divided by its standard deviation.
Nonetheless, being empirically derived these values remain more representative
of psychology research than the typically used *d* = 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8
[e.g., @cohen1992]. Finally, the *Realistic* estimate from which appropriate
sample size is computed here falls close to the effect size implied by
@schäfer2019's estimate of *r* = .16 (translating to *d* &approx;
`r print_d(d_schafer[1L])`) for pre-registered psychology studies.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Effect size for sample size estimation"}
The values in the table above are used by the power analysis to anchor sample
size estimation. Specifically, the *Realistic* scenario *d*~z~ = `r d_real`
serves as the basis for the sample size requirement for detecting the primary
endpoint, i.e., BI~2~ calculated from the first test block. At the necessary
sample size estimated this way, statistical power of the *Best* scenario *d*~z~
= `r d_best` and of the expected BI~3~ effect (*d*~z~ &approx; `r bi3_range`) is
evaluated for informative purposes. Finally, the *Worst* *d*~z~ = `r d_worst`
scenario serves to set the rules for group-sequential top-up sampling if the
primary endpoint fails to be detected at the first look when estimated from a
sample size based on the *Realistic* scenario power analysis (Aim 3, see below).
:::

# Prospective power analysis

The replication study's goal is twofold: (i) to test @beesley2011's original
finding of forward blocking using their BI~2~ on the first test block, and (ii)
to evaluate BI~3~'s suitability as an alternative index of blocking for the
ensuing extension of their results. The power analysis rests only on the former,
which is the only goal that governs declaration of (non-)replication of the
original effect. The power for the latter is then evaluated at the sample size
chosen for the former.

Given the predicted direction of the effect, the replication tests the
original's blocking measure ($\mathbb{E}(BI_2)$) with a one-sided one-sample
*t*-test against no blocking ($\mathbb{E}(BI_2) = 0$) at &alpha; = .05. As
blocking is theoretically justified in persons who successfully learned the
training contingencies and can be contaminated by a tendency to conform to
researchers' expectations in people who already know the phenomenon, all
calculations in this section refer to the Naive analysis set, which serves
as the primary set for `fba-allergy-online-02` analysis.

This section computes the number of participants needed to detect blocking under
each of the scenarios derived above with 80%, 90% and 95% power, and the number
to recruit at the assumed 50% retention. All sample sizes refer to a single,
fixed-sample analysis, without optional stopping; the group-sequential top-up
follows below.

## Sample size

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="R code: Sample size per scenario"}
```{r}
#| label: replication-pwr-sizes
# The replication test: one-sided, at the 5% level (the CIs above use
# `alpha_ci` = .10 for the same reason)
alpha_test <- 0.05
retention_assumed <- 0.50
target_power <- c(0.80, 0.90, 0.95)

scenarios <- c(
  worst = d_worst,
  realistic = d_real,
  best = d_best
)

scenario_labels <- c(
  worst = "Worst",
  realistic = "Realistic",
  best = "Best"
)

# Participants analysed for each scenario and target power, from {pwrss}, with
# an independent check against the exact noncentral t distribution
sizes <-
  tidyr::expand_grid(
    scenario = names(scenarios),
    power = target_power
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    d = unname(scenarios[scenario]),
    n = purrr::map2_dbl(d, power, \(d, p) {
      pwrss::power.t.student(
        d = d,
        power = p,
        alpha = alpha_test,
        alternative = "one.sided",
        design = "one.sample",
        verbose = 0
      )$n
    }),
    recruit = ceiling(n / retention_assumed)
  )

stopifnot(identical(
  as.integer(sizes$n),
  purrr::map2_int(sizes$d, sizes$power, \(d, p) n_one_sample_t(d, p, alpha_test))
))

# Smooth curves of the required sample size across effect sizes (without
# rounding)
curve <-
  tidyr::expand_grid(
    d = seq(0.12, 0.70, by = 0.005),
    power = target_power
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(n = purrr::map2_dbl(d, power, \(d, p) {
    pwrss::power.t.student(
      d = d,
      power = p,
      alpha = alpha_test,
      alternative = "one.sided",
      design = "one.sample",
      ceil.n = FALSE,
      verbose = 0
    )$n
  }))

# Power under the other two scenarios at the sample sizes sized for the
# Realistic one
cross <-
  tidyr::expand_grid(
    target = target_power,
    scenario = c("worst", "best")
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    n = purrr::map_dbl(target, \(p) pick_size(sizes, "realistic", p)),
    d = unname(scenarios[scenario]),
    power = purrr::map2_dbl(d, n, \(d, n) {
      pwrss::power.t.student(
        d = d,
        n2 = n,
        alpha = alpha_test,
        alternative = "one.sided",
        design = "one.sample",
        verbose = 0
      )$power
    })
  )

# Best-scenario power for the text, summarised when it is near 100%
best_power_1 <- round(pick_power(cross, "best", 0.80), 2)
best_power_2 <- round(pick_power(cross, "best", 0.90), 2)
best_power_3 <- round(pick_power(cross, "best", 0.95), 2)

best_power_text <- if (best_power_1 >= 0.99) {
  "99% or more across the sample sizes"
} else {
  sprintf(
    "%s, %s and %s",
    print_power(best_power_1),
    print_power(best_power_2),
    print_power(best_power_3)
  )
}
```
:::

Under the *Realistic* scenario (*d*~z~ = `r d_real`), the replication needs at
minimum `r pick_size(sizes, "realistic", 0.80)`,
`r pick_size(sizes, "realistic", 0.90)` and
`r pick_size(sizes, "realistic", 0.95)` participants in the Naive set for 80%,
90% and 95% power, respectively, yielding
`r pick_size(sizes, "realistic", 0.80, "recruit")`,
`r pick_size(sizes, "realistic", 0.90, "recruit")` and
`r pick_size(sizes, "realistic", 0.95, "recruit")` participants to recruit (see
the table and figure below). If the true effect were as small as in the
*Worst* scenario, these sample sizes would result in the replication having only
`r print_power(pick_power(cross, "worst", 0.80))`,
`r print_power(pick_power(cross, "worst", 0.90))` and
`r print_power(pick_power(cross, "worst", 0.95))` power, respectively. If it
were as large as in the original study (*Best* scenario), power would be
`r best_power_text`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-replication-pwr-sizes
#| tbl-cap: "Sample size required to detect blocking (BI~2~, first test block) under each scenario."
tbl_sample_sizes(
  sizes,
  scenario_labels,
  retention_assumed,
  alpha_test,
  chosen = "Realistic"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-replication-pwr-curve
#| fig-cap: "Sample size required to detect blocking (BI~2~, first test block) with 80%, 90% and 95% power across true effect sizes. The right axis shows the number of participants to recruit at the assumed retention. Dashed lines and labelled points mark the three scenarios. Note the logarithmic scale of the sample size."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
fig_power_curve(
  curve,
  sizes,
  scenario_labels,
  retention_assumed
)
```

## Power of the alternative index

The alternative index, i.e., BI~3~ computed over all six test blocks, is not
used to set the sample size of the study. However, if blocking is detected in
BI~3~, it becomes the blocking index of choice for `fba-allergy-online-03`, and
consequently the power to detect BI~3~-based blocking at the selected sample
size still matters. Assuming BI~3~'s true effect size equals one of the
feasibility study's point estimates, the table below shows the power of the
one-sided *t*-test at the sample sizes under which the BI~2~-based test achieves
80%, 90% and 95% power under the *Realistic* scenario.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="R code: Power of the alternative index"}
```{r}
#| label: replication-pwr-bi3
# BI3 effect sizes of the three analysis sets of the feasibility study, rounded
d_bi3_assumed <- round(d_bi3, 2)

bi3_power <-
  tidyr::expand_grid(
    target = target_power,
    set = names(sets)
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    n = purrr::map_dbl(target, \(p) pick_size(sizes, "realistic", p)),
    d = unname(d_bi3_assumed[set]),
    set = c(full = "Full sample", learned = "Learned set", naive = "Naive set")[set],
    power = purrr::map2_dbl(d, n, \(d, n) {
      pwrss::power.t.student(
        d = d,
        n2 = n,
        alpha = alpha_test,
        alternative = "one.sided",
        design = "one.sample",
        verbose = 0
      )$power
    })
  )
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: tbl-replication-pwr-bi3
#| tbl-cap: "Power of the alternative index test (BI~3~, test blocks 1&ndash;6) at the sample sizes estimated for BI~2~ under the *Realistic* scenario."
tbl_bi3_power(bi3_power, alpha_test)
```

## Group-sequential top-up

If the replication fails to detect blocking with either index, it continues
with a pre-registered top-up of the sample, i.e., a second look at the data
after additional data collection. This makes the study a group-sequential design
[@wassmer2025], in which the rule that sets sample sizes at each look and the
share of the significance level &alpha; each look may spend are fixed in
advance, before the first participant is recruited.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="R code: Group-sequential design"}
```{r}
#| label: replication-pwr-topup
# Look 1 = the replication proper: recruitment of the number calibrated for
# 95% power under the Realistic scenario at the assumed retention, analysed once
# data collection closes, provided the Naive set holds at least the number sized
# for 90% power
n1_recruit <- pick_size(sizes, "realistic", 0.95, "recruit")
n1_min <- pick_size(sizes, "realistic", 0.90)
n1_planned <- pick_size(sizes, "realistic", 0.95)

# Look 2 = the top-up, sized for 80% overall power under the Worst scenario
power_topup_target <- 0.80

# Most of alpha is spent at look 1, the replication proper, so that it keeps
# nearly the power of a single test; look 2 gets the rest
alpha1 <- 0.045

# The rule applied at a range of retention rates, to illustrate how the
# thresholds and the top-up follow the retention look 1 actually achieves
by_retention <- topup_by_retention(
  retention = c(0.40, 0.50, 0.60, 0.75),
  recruit1 = n1_recruit,
  n1_min = n1_min,
  alpha = alpha_test,
  alpha1 = alpha1,
  d = d_worst,
  power = power_topup_target,
  scenarios = scenarios[c("realistic", "worst")]
)

# The design at the assumed retention
planned <- by_retention[abs(by_retention$retention - retention_assumed) < 1e-9, ]
stopifnot(nrow(planned) == 1L, planned$n1 == n1_planned)

# Testing twice at alpha = .05 instead would inflate the false-positive rate
alpha_naive_two_looks <- alpha_two_looks(n1_planned, planned$n2, alpha_test)

# BI3 is tested at the same looks against the same boundaries
design_planned <- design_topup(n1_planned, planned$n2, alpha_test, "fixed", alpha1)
bi3_topup <- purrr::map(
  round(d_bi3, 2),
  \(d) power_topup(design_planned, planned$n2, d)
)
```
:::

**Look 1** is the replication proper. Recruitment closes at `r n1_recruit`
participants, the sample size calibrated for 95% power under the *Realistic*
scenario at the assumed 50% retention. The data are analysed as soon as the
collection is finished, provided the Naive set contains at least `r n1_min`
participants (ensuring 90% power under the *Realistic* scenario). If fewer than
`r n1_min` participants reach the Naive set, recruitment continues in batches
until the minimal required sample size is reached.

**Look 2** happens only if both BI~2~ and BI~3~ analyses fail to detect blocking
at look 1 (see the decision tree below). It is calibrated for 80% overall power
under the *Worst* scenario (*d*~z~ = `r d_worst`). Since testing BI~2~ with the
*p* < .05 threshold at both looks would raise the false-positive rate to about
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * alpha_naive_two_looks)`, the significance level
&alpha; is split between the looks. As look 1 is the replication proper and,
given the prior literature, has good reason to detect blocking as is, I spend
almost all of &alpha; there, fixing &alpha; =
`r sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", alpha1))` at look 1, independently of its
actual sample size. The remaining &alpha; is spent at look 2.

This sequential testing strategy ensures that look 1 keeps nearly the full power
of a single test computed in the previous section, i.e.,
`r print_power(planned$look1_realistic)` under the *Realistic* scenario with
`r n1_planned` participants. As a consequence, look 2 needs a large sample size
to achieve the desired 80% overall power[^3].

[^3]: Note that the calculations assume 90% to 95% power under the *Realistic*
scenario at look 1. However, if this test fails to detect blocking, I shift the
assumptions to the *Worst* scenario, under which look 1's power is
`r print_power(planned$look1_worst)` at best, and top up the sample under this
scenario to achieve 80% power overall, across both looks. In other words, look 1
is calibrated for high power under the *Realistic* scenario, whereas look 2 is
calibrated for acceptable power under the *Worst* scenario with a
group-sequential top-up.

In practice, $\mathbb{E}(BI_2)$ is significantly greater than zero at look 1
if its one-sided *p* < `r sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", alpha1))`, and at look 2
if the one-sided *p* of all participants of the Naive set falls below a nominal
level of about `r sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", planned$p2))` (see the table
below). Its exact value depends on the sample sizes actually reached at look 1
and is computed once they are known, here and below with the `{rpact}` package
[@wassmer2026].

**In summary, I fix the significance level at look 1 to *p* <
`r sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", alpha1))`, allowing the power to vary within
acceptable bounds assuming the *Realistic* scenario, but I fix the overall power
under the *Worst* scenario at 80%, allowing the significance threshold to
vary depending on the observed retention rate.**

```{r}
#| label: tbl-replication-pwr-topup-thresholds
#| tbl-cap: "Illustration of the pre-registered top-up rule applied at four retention rates."
tbl_topup_thresholds(by_retention, n1_recruit, power_topup_target)
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Rules of the top-up for pre-registration"}
- **The rule, not the number, is pre-registered.** Look 2 calibrates the Naive
  analysis set to the smallest sample that yields 80% overall power under the
  *Worst* scenario, given &alpha; = `r sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", alpha1))`
  at look 1 and the look-1 sample size reached.
- **Only outcome-blind quantities enter the rule**, i.e., the look-1 sample and
  the retention. The look-1 estimate of blocking is not considered when
  computing look 2 sample size requirements.
- **The critical values are recomputed** for the sample sizes actually reached
  at each look, keeping &alpha; = `r sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", alpha1))` at
  look 1 and an overall &alpha; = `r sub("^0", "", format(alpha_test))`.
- **Look 2 is skipped when BI~2~ analysis detects blocking at look 1**, in which
  case replication is declared successful and *d*~z~ is estimated with its 95%
  CI for the ensuing extension study (which, unlike the replication, tests
  against a two-sided alternative hypothesis).
- **The interim analysis at look 1 is the only planned look at BI~2~** before
  look 2. Attrition, completion time and the yield of the learning check may be
  monitored throughout.
- **After look 2, the effect size is reported as the median-unbiased
  estimate** with its confidence interval under the stage-wise ordering. Both
  correct the bias that a naive estimate carries after a sequential design.
- **BI~3~ is tested in parallel at both looks against the same boundaries.**
  At look 1, BI~3~ reaches `r print_power(bi3_topup$full[["look1"]])` power if
  its true effect equals the Full sample estimate and
  `r print_power(bi3_topup$learned[["look1"]])` if it equals the Learned set
  estimate.
- **Look 2 is skipped when BI~3~ analysis detects blocking at look 1, even if
  BI~2~ fails to do so.** This is the only rule that stops the study without
  rejecting the null hypothesis for BI~2~, so it cannot raise its false-positive
  rate.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Practical caps on the sample size"}
- **A cap on look 2.** If the look 2 rule asks for more participants than the
  LABELS pool can supply in one semester, a cap will be fixed at the number of
  participants available, and the power it achieves will be reported.
- **Look 1 below its minimum.** If fewer than the `r n1_min` minimum
  participants reach the Naive set during look-1 data collection, the sampling
  will continue in smaller batches, aiming at recruiting the additional
  participants necessary to reach the `r n1_planned` planned Naive set
  participants given the retention rate observed until then. This process
  continues until at least `r n1_min` participants reach the Naive set.
:::
